definition.text: This card's subtitle bundles two concerns this repo's own architecture keeps as separate capability rows: an approval decision (a human or a policy gate saying an output may proceed) and provenance (a signed statement about that output). Only the second half has a named contract on this card. This repo's own target states the provenance contract as: "Every artifact is attributable to the code version, inputs and actor that produced it, verifiable with a tool we did not write" (F-b4-05), and names its standard and today's adapter in the same table: "in-toto · SLSA · DSSE | JSONL evidence records | Sigstore · any attestation store" (F-b3-12). So Admit, on its provenance half, is the step that turns a validated result (5.1) into a signed, outside-checkable statement before it is returned (5.3) -- the approval half has no equivalent sourced definition on this card and is carried into gaps.

evidence.quote: Every artifact is attributable to the code version, inputs and actor that produced it, verifiable with a tool we did not write
in-toto · SLSA · DSSE | JSONL evidence records | Sigstore · any attestation store

standards.role: The statement format an admitted output's provenance would be recorded in: a fixed, lightweight Statement carrying a predicate and one or more subjects, the layer directly above the DSSE envelope.
standards.covers: in-toto's own predicate catalogue and worked examples are generic build/source/package software-supply-chain claims -- 'nothing in the README or the predicate list names a prompt, an agent, a routing table, or a playbook' (this repo's own finding, X-refmodel-7-4-promote-007) -- so admitting an agent-generated output is not a use its published vocabulary already covers.

evidence.text:
in-toto's own spec defines the Statement as "the middle layer of the attestation, binding it to a
particular subject and unambiguously identifying the types of the
[Predicate]" -- concretely a JSON object with a required `subject` array (artifacts matched by content digest) and a required `predicateType` URI naming the schema of an optional `predicate` object.

evidence.quote: The Statement is the middle layer of the attestation, binding it to a particular subject and unambiguously identifying the types of the Predicate.

standards.role: Names the specific predicate type (SLSA Provenance v1.0/v1.1) an outside verifier expects when checking build-style provenance, signed via DSSE and bound to an artifact through the subject field.
standards.covers: SLSA's own worked example is a software build platform (builder identity, build instructions, dependency digests) -- not a human-or-policy admit decision over a generated artifact that was never compiled.

evidence.text: SLSA Provenance v1.0 is a predicate type within the in-toto framework. When a SLSA-compliant build platform generates provenance, it produces an in-toto attestation with predicateType: https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1, signs it with DSSE, and associates it with the built artifact via the subject field.

evidence.quote: This document defines the following predicate type within the in-toto attestation framework: "predicateType": "https://slsa.dev/provenance/v1"

standards.role: The signing envelope an in-toto statement travels in: a lightweight container for signed payloads that provides signature verification without embedding public keys, the mechanism that lets an outside tool check the seal without our cooperation.
standards.covers: DSSE only wraps and signs; it says nothing about who may approve an output or when a statement is written, so it covers none of this card's 'Approve' half.

evidence.text: An in-toto attestation has two layers: the DSSE envelope and the statement. DSSE is a lightweight container format for signed payloads standardized at secure-systems-lab. DSSE provides signature verification without embedding public keys in the attestation, enabling portable verification by external tools.

evidence.quote: DSSE is a lightweight container format for signed payloads standardized at secure-systems-lab.

tools.name: This repo's own evidence ledger (kb/ledger.jsonl, written and read by tools/kb.py)
tools.note: Matches F-b3-12's named target adapter, 'JSONL evidence records', by shape: append-only, hash-chained, and each record this repo actually writes carries a git_commit, an agent field and an inputs list (verified by inspecting kb/ledger.jsonl directly). It is genuinely running -- `python3 tools/kb.py ledger-verify` is a live command in this repo. But it is checked only by kb.py, the tool that wrote it, so it does not meet F-b4-05's own bar of 'verifiable with a tool we did not write': there is no outside verifier, no signature and no transparency log standing behind it.

evidence.text: | **Provenance** | in-toto · SLSA · DSSE | JSONL evidence records | Sigstore · any attestation store |

tools.name: Sigstore (cosign, Rekor, Fulcio)
tools.note: Named swap candidate for provenance in this repo's own target table (F-b3-12); provides exactly the external-verifier mechanism this repo's own ledger currently lacks -- keyless signing plus a public, append-only transparency log a third party can check independent of the signer.

evidence.text: Sigstore provides keyless signing through ephemeral key signing where users verify artifacts using a transparency log for signature verification rather than keys. Sigstore's keyless methods include Fulcio (certificate authority for short-lived signing certificates issued based on OpenID Connect identity) and Rekor (transparency log recording every signature in a non-modifiable way).

evidence.quote: A Sigstore client, such as Cosign, creates a public/private key pair and makes a certificate signing request to our code-signing certificate authority (Fulcio) with the public key. A verifiable OpenID Connect (OIDC) identity token is also provided in the request.

tools.name: GitHub Actions Artifact Attestations
tools.note: Real production example of provenance moving from an opt-in extra to a default, always-on pipeline behaviour for public repositories -- evidence that the industry direction is toward attestation-by-default rather than attestation-on-request, which bears on whether Admit should be an optional post-hoc step or a mandatory stage.

evidence.text: GitHub has been steadily tightening enforcement through 2025 and into 2026, and for public repositories, attestation generation is shifting from opt-in to default behavior.

evidence.quote: attestation generation is shifting from opt-in to default behavior

landscape.text: The provenance half of this card sits on real, adopted standards -- in-toto's Statement/predicate/subject structure, SLSA's build-provenance predicate, DSSE's signing envelope -- that this repo's own target table already names together (F-b3-12) and that industry is moving toward enforcing by default rather than on request (X-maturity-a-005). The real tradeoff is not which standard to adopt (this repo has already picked one triad) but what predicate an agent's admitted OUTPUT would use: every source found describes this stack's worked examples as software builds and packages, and this repo's own research explicitly checked and found no published predicate or schema for 'an agent/prompt/tool-routing promotion or release record' (X-refmodel-7-4-promote-007) -- so adopting in-toto/SLSA/DSSE here means authoring a new predicate type, not reusing an existing one. Separately, this repo's own current implementation (the JSONL evidence ledger) already satisfies the append-only and attributable-fields half of the contract but not the externally-verifiable half, which is exactly the gap Sigstore's keyless-signing-plus-transparency-log model exists to close.

evidence.quote: in-toto · SLSA · DSSE | JSONL evidence records | Sigstore · any attestation store
The in-toto Attestation Framework provides a specification for generating verifiable claims about any aspect of how a piece of software is produced.
attestation generation is shifting from opt-in to default behavior

usage.text: No target fact defines a call signature for this card by name. Proposed, following the provenance contract's own shape (F-b4-05, F-b3-12): a caller submits one validated result (the Judge verdict from 5.1) plus the artifact it decided about; Admit's approval half returns an allow/deny (this repo's own cap-policy contract: 'a structured request in, a deterministic allow or deny plus the deciding rule out, before anything is spent' -- proposed reuse, not yet checked against this card) or routes to a human via cap-human-interaction's approval gate; on allow, Admit's provenance half writes one attestation binding the artifact to its code version, inputs and actor, and returns a reference to that attestation, never the attestation's private signing material.

gaps.what: This card's subtitle bundles 'Approve outputs' and 'Store provenance' -- a decision and a record -- which this repo's own architecture keeps as separate capabilities: cap-human-interaction and cap-policy own the decision; cap-provenance owns the record. Nothing found here justifies merging them onto one reference-model card, echoing the same pattern flagged on card 2.4.
gaps.why_it_matters: A caller could read this card as one mechanism when it is at least two independently swappable ones -- an approval gate can change (human review today, a policy engine tomorrow) without touching how provenance is recorded, and vice versa.
gaps.research_query: kb_index.py search "cap-human-interaction cap-policy cap-provenance admit boundary approval before record"

gaps.what: in-toto and SLSA's own published scope and worked examples are software builds and packages. This repo's own prior research explicitly searched for and did not find a predicate or schema for an agent/prompt/routing/promotion record (X-refmodel-7-4-promote-007).
gaps.why_it_matters: Citing in-toto/SLSA/DSSE as 'the standard' for Admit is accurate for the envelope and signing mechanism but overstates coverage: the actual predicate content for 'what was admitted and why' would be this repo's own design, not an adopted schema, until a predicate type is authored and, ideally, registered.
gaps.research_query: has any project defined and published an in-toto predicate type for an LLM/agent output review or promotion decision

gaps.what: DSSE has no fetched (status: fetched) research record in this corpus as of this writing -- the sole record found, X-xc-provenance-chain-002, is status: search-only (a title and search-result snippet, no page body retrieved), unlike in-toto and SLSA's promotion research which include a fetched record (X-refmodel-7-4-promote-007).
gaps.why_it_matters: This is a real, currently-standing evidence gap, not a hypothetical one: DSSE is cited on this card at the weakest evidence grade this repo's own research schema recognises, one step below the other two legs of the same standard triad.
gaps.research_query: capture https://github.com/secure-systems-lab/dsse (or its README) directly and write a fetched research record

gaps.what: This repo's own running evidence ledger (kb/ledger.jsonl) already resembles a provenance mechanism -- it is append-only, hash-chained, and each record carries a git_commit, an actor (agent field) and an inputs list -- but it is verified only by kb.py, a tool this repo wrote itself, not by an outside party.
gaps.why_it_matters: F-b4-05's own bar for provenance is 'verifiable with a tool we did not write.' By that bar this repo's most Admit-like existing mechanism does not yet qualify as provenance at all, which is a sharper and more specific finding than simply marking the card planned.
gaps.research_query: would running slsa-verifier or an in-toto verification tool against a DSSE-wrapped export of kb/ledger.jsonl records constitute meeting F-b4-05's bar, or does the ledger's own hash-chain format need to change first

gaps.what: No sourced definition exists anywhere in this corpus for what the 'Approve' decision itself checks -- the criterion an output must meet to be admitted is undefined here; only how a decision would later be recorded (provenance) has a contract.
gaps.why_it_matters: A card that specifies the record format for a decision but not the decision's own criterion cannot yet be implemented end to end; a caller would have to invent the approval logic from scratch.
gaps.research_query: kb_index.py search "cap-policy operation allow deny criterion output approval before spend"
